newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine ministers covered up corruption - Cavallo.
newsitem.headline: Argentine ministers covered up corruption - Cavallo.

text.p: Former Argentine Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo, fired in July by President Carlos Menem, on Tuesday accused two government ministers of covering up corruption and manipulating judges.

Cavallo told a radio station that Interior Minister Carlos Corach had tried to remove a judge from investigating a gold-export fraud case and replace him with another magistrate "who failed to find any crime committed by gold exporters."
Both Corach and Justice Minister Elias Jassan were manipulating judges and state prosecutors, alleged Cavallo, the architect of Argentina's economic reform plan.

Corach once wrote on a paper napkin the name of several judges and state prosecutors and bragged, "These do as I say", said Cavallo, sacked last July after one of many clashes with Menem over his austerity policies.
"Jassan used to call judges and prosecutors to give them instructions on issues he was interested in," he said from New York, where he is teaching economics at a university.
"There is a feeling of a lack of security or justice in Argentina," said Cavallo, who last week announced he will run for Congress in 1997, but not for Menem's Peronist Party.

The charges of Cavallo, who as minister faced fire from the ruling party for alleging that "mafias" had penetrated the public service, prompted a flurry of criticism and denials. He had clashed before with the interior minister.
"All courts in the country are open," Menem said, challenging Cavallo to back his accusations with evidence.
In a statement, Corach rejected the charges, calling them "totally irresponsible and reflecting (Cavallo's) state of emotional imbalance." He also said he would take legal action.
A spokesman for Jassan said the justice minister had no immediate plans to react to Cavallo's charges.
Federal judge Adolfo Bagnasco dared Cavallo to present the napkin as evidence. "All else is heresay, resembling more a Mexican soap opera than any other thing," he said.
Opposition leaders alleged Cavallo was also tainted by the same charges he levelled against his former colleagues.
Rodolfo Terragno, chairman of the main opposition force, the Radical Party, agreed. "We are witnessing a rupture between mafias, not an accusation against the mafia," he said.

Cavallo triggered a major scandal last year when he charged in Congress that there were "mafias" infiltrated in the government trying to seek a monopoly on public services such as the post office for criminal ends.

On Tuesday he accused Corach of trying to remove public prosecutor Pablo Lanusse from a case involving firms buying gold and re-exporting it, fraudulently claiming $70 million in subsidies, in a bid to stonewall investigators.
